fetched_contents.text: Optimization of wastes content in ceramic tiles using statistical design of mixture experiments Abstract Mineral extraction and processing industries have been cited as sources of environmental contamination and pollution. The inclusion of wastes into productive cycles represents an alternative form of restoration, which is interesting from both environmental and economic standpoints. In this work, the development of ceramic tile formulations containing kaolin processing and granite sawing wastes was investigated using the statistical design of mixture experiments methodology. Ten formulations using the raw materials, red clay, kaolin processing and granite sawing wastes, were selected and used in the mixture design. Test specimens were fired and characterized to determine their water absorption, linear firing shrinkage and modulus of rupture. Regression models were calculated, correlating the properties with the composition. The significance and validity of the models were confirmed by statistical analysis and verification experiments. The regression models were used to optimize the waste content in ceramic compositions. The results showed that formulations containing up to 62% of waste could be used in the production of ceramic tiles. Introduction Economic and demographic growth demands increasingly high indices of industrial activity, which implies two major environmental problems. First, it ultimately feeds on natural non-renewable resources that are becoming scarce and will be sooner or later depleted; and second, it produces increasing amounts of waste materials, which are more and more difficult to dispose of.1 Around the world, millions of tons of inorganic wastes are produced every day. Traditionally, these wastes have been disposed of in landfills and often dumped directly into ecosystems without adequate treatment. However, possible reuse or recycling alternatives should be investigated and implemented.2, 3, 4 The inclusion of wastes into alternative productive cycles may represent an alternative form of reclamation, which is interesting from the environmental and economic standpoints. Restoration and recycling is the best environmental solution to save raw materials and to reduce the amount of industrial wastes discarded.5, 6, 7 Thus, the search for new recycling technologies is of high technological, economic and environmental interest.8 In this regard, interesting opportunities are found in the traditional ceramics industry, particularly the sector devoted to the fabrication of building products. Natural raw materials used in the fabrication of clay-based ceramic products show a wide range of compositional variations and the resulting products are very heterogeneous. Therefore, such products can tolerate further compositional fluctuations and raw material changes, allowing different types of wastes to be incorporated into ceramic tiles and bricks.1, 9, 10 Kaolin is an important raw material in various industrial sectors. However the kaolin mining and processing industry produces large amounts of waste. The kaolin industry, which processes primary kaolin, produces two types of wastes. The first type derives from the first processing step (separation of sand from ore). The second type of waste results from the second processing step, which consists of wet sieving to separate the finer fraction and purify the kaolin. The granite processing industry also generates large amounts of wastes worldwide. Granite sawing waste contains feldspar, quartz and mica as major constituents and metallic dust and lime (used as abrasive and lubricant, respectively) as residual materials. Various studies9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 have demonstrated the viability of using granite sawing waste in the production of ceramic tiles. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study has investigated the potential use of granite waste in combination with kaolin processing waste to produce ceramic tiles. The current optimization procedure for developing ceramic compositions using waste materials consists of an experimental rather than a comprehensive approach. In general, the approach involves selecting and testing a first trial batch, evaluating the results, and then adjusting the mixture's proportions and testing further mixtures until the required properties are achieved. The conventional method of optimization is time consuming and does not allow the global optimum to be detected, particularly due to interactions among the variables. In contrast, statistical design methods are rigorous techniques both to achieve desired properties and to establish an optimized mixture for a given constraint, while minimizing the number of trials.16, 17 In the development and manufacture of ceramics using waste materials the properties of fired bodies are determined basically by the combination of raw materials and process parameters. When the processing conditions are kept constant, a number of properties of dried and fired bodies are determined principally by the combination (or mixture) of raw materials.18 That is the basic assumption in the statistical design of mixture experiments to obtain a response surface using mathematical and statistical techniques.19, 20 To this end, it is necessary first to select the appropriate mixtures from which the response surface might be calculated. With the response surface in hand, a prediction of the property value can then be obtained for any mixture, based on changes in the proportions of its components.18, 21. This methodology has found important applications in various areas and is becoming popular in the field of glasses and ceramics.18, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 In every reported case, the methodology has led to greater efficiency and confidence in the results obtained21 and has simultaneously optimized the content of raw materials with a minimum of experiments. Submission received: 19 February 2021 / Revised: 16 March 2021 / Accepted: 18 March 2021 / Published: 23 March 2021 Abstract Mullite (3Al2O3·2SiO2) is an aluminosilicate characterized by excellent physical properties, which makes it an important ceramic material. In this way, ceramics based on mullite find applications in different technological fields as refractory material (metallurgy, glass, ceramics, etc.), matrix in composite materials for high temperature applications, substrate in multilayer packaging, protective coatings, components of turbine engines, windows transparent to infrared radiation, etc. However, mullite is scarce in nature so it has to be manufactured through different synthesis methods, such as sintering, melting-crystallization or through a sol-gel route. Commonly, mullite is fabricated from pure technical grade raw materials, making the manufacturing process expensive. An alternative to lowering the cost is the use of mining waste as silica (SiO2) and alumina (Al2O3) feedstock, which are the necessary chemical compounds required to manufacture mullite ceramics. In addition to the economic benefits, the use of mining waste brings out environmental benefits as it prevents the over-exploitation of natural resources and reduces the volume of mining waste that needs to be managed. This article reviews the scientific studies carried out in order to use waste (steriles and tailings) generated in mining activities for the manufacture of clay-based ceramic materials containing mullite as a main crystalline phase. 1. Introduction Nowadays, mining is a critical industry for global economic and social development, and it will continue to be the main resources provider in the immediate future [1]. However, just as there have been great technological advances in mining techniques that allow a larger recovery of minerals and therefore a continuous growth of world production, the impoverishment of deposits in terms of the grade, which requires larger scale, more complex and depth excavations, has an even higher impact on a major generation of waste. Thus, mining activities imply the generation of huge amounts of mining waste that produce great impacts on the environment, among others instability in waste dumps, acid drainage mainly due to oxidation processes, water pollution, air pollution and a long etcetera, which also includes the huge extents of territory occupied by the deposits of residues from the mineral washing and flotation plants [10,11]. Worldwide, there are approximately 3500 solid mining waste facilities, with an estimated generation of over 100 billion tons per year [12]. An idea of the magnitude of waste generated is given by the fact that, for example, in the case of iron or aluminum mining, the amount of solid waste generated is several times greater than the mass of the metals extracted, but in the case of noble metals such as gold, this ratio is greater than millions of times [13,14]. Tayebi-Khorami et al. [12] in an interesting study on the current management frameworks of mining waste, established the need for the mining industry to develop strategies in the medium and short term for proper management and use of waste aimed at achieving a lower environmental impact. The design and implementation of robust long-term solutions remains, to date, a challenge for the mining industry, due to the specificity of the sites where wastes are generated, the local weather conditions and the physicochemical heterogeneity of their wastes [15]. Besides, the global megatrends (large, social, economic, political, environmental, or technological changes) as driving technology demands should be taking into consideration by the mining industry for its future economic growth [16]. Solid mining waste is grouped into two main groups, viz mine waste rock (steriles) and tailings. Mine waste rock consists of low-grade excavated bedrock that has been transported to access profitable ore, and generally comprises of relatively coarse broken granular rock in the size range from sand to pebbles or boulders. They are mainly piled on high mounds which are porous, hydraulically unsaturated, and therefore highly exposed to atmospheric conditions (oxidation). Tailings are the main waste, both in volume and weight, generated in the process of concentrating minerals. fetched_contents.text: Residues from beneficiation of granite in porcelain stoneware: Effects on technological properties 1. Introduction Granite rocks have long been exploited for a wide range of applications, including ornamental stone [1], quartz-feldspathic flux for vitrified ceramics [[2], [3], [4], [5]], crushed aggregates for concrete and mortar [6,7], boulders and ballast for civil engineering [8,9]. Extraction and processing to achieve the technical specifications for the various uses of granite generate different kinds of waste [10]. Each of them has specific chemical and physical characteristics, which affect the possibility of recycling that can be expressed in terms of technology readiness level (TRL). * • Quarry residues are basically made of blocks that do meet the requirements for ornamental stone and fine-grained tails. The former waste is currently reused (TRL 9) as ceramic flux [[11], [12], [13], [14]] or in civil engineering, e.g., as boulders for outer dam and breakwater in ports [15]. The fine-grained tails have been investigated as ceramic raw material as well [16]. * • Residues of cutting, sawing and polishing operations on ornamental stone consist essentially of powdered granite, contaminated by grinding media and additives: the main issue is the increased values of Fe2O3, CaO and pH [17,18]. Attempts have been spent for the valorisation of these residues in ceramic products of various types, including clay bricks and roof tiles, wall and floor tiles and lightweight aggregates [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24]]. As far as we know, this waste is only occasionally used by the ceramic industry in red-body products, mainly bricks [[25], [26], [27], [28]], while for whiteware the TRL is around 5–6. * • Fractions discarded by the beneficiation of quartz-feldspathic flux (mostly for porcelain stoneware tiles, but also glazes, sanitary ware and container glass) are typically composed of granite enriched in femic minerals, e.g., biotite, amphiboles, Fe-oxides [[29], [30], [31]]. The mineralurgical processes that are commonly used [[32], [33], [34], [35]] are grinding and sieving (to achieve mineral liberation) and high field intensity magnetic separation or less frequently froth flotation (to achieve the separation of iron-bearing minerals). The resulting residues can be relatively coarse-grained (magnetic fraction) or fine-grained (flotation tailings, dust from air cleaning of the treatment plant). As far as we know, the level of technological readiness for recycling these types of waste is low, probably around TRL 2. In the processing of granites, to obtain 100,000 tons of feldspar product, the amount of waste generated is typically about 12 thousand tons of magnetic fraction and about 7 thousand tons of dust from air cleaning [13]. Considering that the world production of feldspar from granites is around 3.6 million tons per year [5], the global yearly output of residues can be approximately estimated at 250,000 tons (dust from air cleaning) and 430,000 tons (magnetic fraction). While the recycling of residues from quarrying, sawing and polishing of ornamental granite has already been the subject of many studies, detailed investigation on the behaviour of beneficiation waste in the ceramic process is not available. To fill this gap, laboratory-scale experiments were carried out to reveal the technological behaviour of coarse-grained (magnetic fraction) and fine-grained (dust from air cleaning) residues in the manufacture of porcelain stoneware tiles. The main limitation of the magnetic fraction is its high iron oxide content, which affects colour but can also cause aesthetic defects in ceramics, such as speckling and unwanted stains [30,36,37]. High iron levels have been ascribed for defects such as black core and bloating [[38], [39], [40]]. It is necessary to understand if there are technological constraints in the design of sustainable bodies, which can tolerate a darker colour or speckling, to be used in “green” tiles [[41], [42], [43]]. The problem with de-dusting waste is handling a very fine-grained powder, which is difficult to mix with the other ingredients of the batch and can affect compaction and drying operations, reducing the air permeability of compacts [44,45]. It would be useful to understand to what extent these drawbacks can be tolerated in novel sustainable batches for ceramic tiles [43,46]. Granite waste alters the raw material system and processing of porcelain tiles by replacing or modifying traditional raw materials, changing melting behavior, viscosity, green-body workability, and the sintering window and firing temperature regime.

First, granite waste can replace or modify traditional porcelain-tile raw materials by acting as a secondary raw material in ceramic tile formulations. The evidence shows that granite sawing waste contains feldspar, quartz, and mica as major constituents, along with metallic dust and lime as residual materials, making it a chemically meaningful addition to ceramic bodies [N1-F1]. A separate study on granite-waste porcelain stoneware also reports that beneficiation residues from granite include coarse-grained magnetic fractions and fine-grained dust from air cleaning, which were evaluated as secondary raw materials for porcelain stoneware tiles [N3-F3]. This suggests that granite waste can substitute or supplement traditional porcelain-tile raw materials such as ball clay, quartz sand, and feldspar, rather than simply being a filler or contaminant [N3-F3].

Second, granite waste affects melting behavior and viscosity during sintering. The direct evidence indicates that granite waste addition can shift sintering behavior: the SD addition promoted sintering phenomena and increased densification for additions of 6–9% [N5-R1]. The sintering mechanisms of porcelain stoneware also describe a viscous-flow mechanism as dominant over 1100 °C, with densification controlled by the viscosity of the liquid phase [N5-F4]. Because granite waste often contains quartz and feldspar, which can contribute to the glassy phase and melt development, it can alter the viscosity and melting window of the body. The review on mullite-based ceramics from mining waste further notes that the introduction of Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ feedstocks is central to manufacturing mullite ceramics, and that additives can change the mullite-formation reaction mechanism [N2-F2]. Although the evidence does not explicitly identify granite waste as the additive in that review, the underlying principle is relevant: raw-material composition shifts can modify phase reactions and melt behavior.

Third, granite waste affects green-body workability. The evidence on granite-waste porcelain stoneware notes that the main limitation of the magnetic fraction is its high iron oxide content, which can affect color and cause aesthetic defects, and that de-dusting waste is difficult to mix with other ingredients, reducing air permeability of compacts [N3-F3]. This implies that granite waste can complicate wet mixing, compaction, and drying operations. In porcelain-tile processing, green-body workability depends on particle size distribution, surface area, and binder interactions, and the evidence suggests that granite waste fractions can introduce handling challenges that affect the uniformity and compactibility of the batch [N3-F3].

Fourth, granite waste can shift the sintering window and firing temperature regime. The direct evidence indicates that granite-waste additions promoted sintering phenomena and increased densification at 6–9% addition [N5-R1]. The porcelain-stoneware sintering study also states that densification occurs over 1100 °C and is controlled by melt viscosity and solubility of solids in the liquid phase, while coarsening and solubility of gases become important in the final stage [N5-F4]. In porcelain-tile bodies, firing temperature is typically constrained by the need to achieve vitrification and low porosity without excessive melting. The evidence here suggests that granite waste can narrow or shift the sintering window because it can lower the onset of densification, alter the melt viscosity, and change the temperature range over which viscous flow and coarsening operate [N5-R1][N5-F4].

Overall, granite waste modifies the porcelain-tile raw material system by replacing or supplementing traditional ingredients, changing melting behavior and viscosity, affecting green-body workability, and shifting the sintering window and firing temperature regime [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-F4].

Granite waste influences mullite formation and microstructure by altering the phase-composition environment, promoting or modifying mullite formation conditions, and changing crystallinity and pore structure during sintering.

First, granite waste can influence mullite formation by providing Al₂O₃ and SiO₂, which are essential chemical components of mullite (3Al₂O₃·2SiO₂). The review on mullite-based ceramics from mining waste states that mullite is manufactured from pure technical-grade raw materials, and that mining waste can be used as a source of SiO₂ and Al₂O₃ feedstock [N2-F2]. While the direct evidence does not explicitly identify granite waste as the source of Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ in the porcelain-tile context, the principle is relevant: granite waste can contribute the necessary chemical constituents for mullite formation. The same review also notes that the introduction of V₂O₅ and AlF₃ changed the mullite-formation reaction mechanism and significantly reduced the sintering temperature [N2-R1]. This implies that granite-waste-derived additions can, in principle, alter the kinetics and conditions under which mullite forms, even if the evidence here is not a direct granite-waste-to-mullite study.

Second, granite waste can affect phase composition and crystallinity. The porcelain-stoneware sintering study describes a body composition of ball clay, quartz sand, and sodium or potassium feldspar, with a glassy matrix and residual crystalline phases such as quartz, feldspars, and newly formed mullite [N5-F4]. It also states that the main transformations include breakdown of clay minerals and formation of amorphous components, followed by mullite and viscous phase over 1000 °C [N5-F4]. Granite waste can modify this phase sequence by adding quartz, feldspar, and mica, which may either support or compete with mullite nucleation and growth. The evidence also notes that the addition of talc in a related study decreased porosity after compaction and lowered firing temperature, suggesting that additives can influence phase evolution [N3-R5]. While talc is not granite waste, this principle supports the idea that granite-waste additions can change the crystalline and amorphous balance in the body.

Third, granite waste can affect pore structure and porosity. The porcelain-stoneware study emphasizes that residual closed porosity is a major limitation in porcelain stoneware, consisting of 2–8% closed pores, and that this porosity is detrimental to mechanical and tribological properties [N5-F4]. The direct granite-waste evidence on porcelain stoneware reports that granite beneficiation residues were evaluated in porcelain stoneware tiles and that handling such fine-grained dust can reduce air permeability of compacts [N3-F3]. In addition, a separate study on granite-waste porcelain tiles reports that increasing granite sludge from 10 to 40 wt% increases bulk density from 1.86 to 2.69 g/cm³ and apparent porosity decreases from 40 to 15% [N3-R2]. This suggests that granite waste can reduce porosity by densifying the body, but the evidence also shows that porosity reduction is not always linear and can depend on the fraction and type of granite waste [N3-R2]. The sintering mechanisms study further explains that densification occurs by particle rearrangement and viscous flow over 1100 °C, and that coarsening and solubility of gases become important in the final stage [N5-F4]. This means that pore elimination during sintering is not simply a direct consequence of granite waste addition; it is mediated by viscosity, melt development, and phase-coarsening behavior.

Fourth, the relationship between mullite and pore elimination during sintering appears indirect but important. The porcelain-stoneware study states that the main limit of the product is residual porosity, which is detrimental to mechanical and tribological properties [N5-F4]. The same study identifies mullite as a newly formed crystalline phase that forms over 1000 °C, while viscous phase and coarsening dominate later stages [N5-F4]. Granite waste can contribute to pore elimination by densifying the body and reducing porosity, as shown by the direct granite-waste porcelain-stoneware evidence [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also suggests that pore elimination is not solely driven by mullite formation; it is also driven by viscous flow, particle rearrangement, and solubility of solids and gases [N5-F4]. Thus, mullite can support pore elimination by contributing to the glassy matrix and crystalline framework, but pore elimination is a broader sintering outcome that depends on viscosity, melt behavior, and phase evolution [N5-F4][N3-R2].

In summary, granite waste influences mullite formation and microstructure by supplying Al₂O₃ and SiO₂, modifying phase composition, and changing crystallinity and pore structure during sintering [N2-F2][N5-F4][N3-R2]. The evidence indicates that mullite formation can be altered by additive chemistry, but pore elimination during sintering is a more complex process involving viscous flow, particle rearrangement, and phase coarsening [N2-R1][N5-F4].

Long-term durability and performance tradeoffs of granite-waste porcelain tiles are shaped by water absorption, weathering resistance, thermal cycling, and dimensional stability, with implications for indoor and outdoor use.

First, water absorption is a key durability indicator. The evidence shows that porcelain tiles are classified as impervious, absorbing 0.5% or less moisture, and that porcelain tile is inherently water-resistant due to its dense, vitrified structure [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The porcelain-tile versus ceramic-tile comparison also states that porcelain tiles absorb ≤0.5% water compared to ceramic tiles absorbing more than 3% [N6-R3]. This means that porcelain tiles are generally highly water-resistant, but the evidence also suggests that granite-waste porcelain tiles may differ: the granite-waste porcelain-stoneware study reports that increasing granite sludge from 10 to 40 wt% decreases apparent porosity from 40 to 15% [N3-R2]. A lower porosity can improve water resistance, but the evidence does not directly quantify water absorption in granite-waste porcelain tiles. Therefore, the durability implication is that granite-waste porcelain tiles may retain or even improve water resistance compared to conventional porcelain tiles, depending on how porosity is reduced [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R2].

Second, weathering resistance is another durability concern. The evidence indicates that porcelain tile has low water absorption and is durable in wet and moisture-prone environments, and that it is used in high-demand spaces because of its low absorption rate and durability [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The same granite-waste porcelain-stoneware evidence notes that the magnetic fraction can cause aesthetic defects such as speckling and unwanted stains, and that handling fine-grained dust can reduce air permeability and complicate mixing [N3-F3]. These issues suggest that weathering resistance may be compromised if granite waste introduces color instability, surface defects, or uneven microstructure. In other words, the tradeoff is that granite-waste porcelain tiles can retain good water resistance, but they may be more prone to weathering-related defects such as discoloration or staining if the waste fraction is not carefully controlled [N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3].

Third, thermal cycling and dimensional stability are important for durability. The porcelain-stoneware sintering study notes that densification occurs over 1100 °C and that the final stage involves coarsening and solubility of gases, which can affect microstructure [N5-F4]. It also states that residual closed porosity is detrimental to flexural modulus of rupture and abrasion resistance, and that the main limit of porcelain stoneware is its residual porosity [N5-F4]. Thermal cycling can exacerbate this by causing stress relaxation, cracking, or microcrack propagation, especially in materials with residual porosity or uneven microstructure. The evidence does not directly measure thermal cycling performance for granite-waste porcelain tiles, but it does indicate that porosity and microstructure strongly influence dimensional stability and mechanical performance [N5-F4]. This implies that granite-waste porcelain tiles may have tradeoffs in thermal cycling resistance: lower porosity can improve dimensional stability, but uneven phase distribution or coarsening can reduce it [N5-F4].

Fourth, durability implications for indoor versus outdoor use are mixed. Porcelain tiles are generally suitable for both indoor and outdoor use because of their low water absorption and durability [N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, granite-waste porcelain tiles may have different performance characteristics. The evidence shows that granite-waste additions can reduce porosity and improve densification [N3-R2], which is favorable for outdoor use. At the same time, granite-waste residues can introduce color and aesthetic defects, such as black core, bloating, speckling, and unwanted stains [N3-F3]. These issues are more likely to affect indoor use, where appearance and surface quality are critical, than outdoor use, where weathering resistance is more important [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore suggests that granite-waste porcelain tiles can be durable for outdoor applications, but they may require careful control of waste composition to avoid indoor-use defects [N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3].

Overall, the long-term durability and performance tradeoffs of granite-waste porcelain tiles are positive in terms of water resistance and reduced porosity, but they can also introduce aesthetic and microstructural risks such as weathering defects, color instability, and uneven microstructure [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R2][N3-F3]. Thermal cycling and dimensional stability depend on porosity and microstructure, and the material is likely to perform better outdoors than indoors when defects are minimized [N5-F4].

Granite waste affects porcelain tiles by modifying the raw material system, changing microstructure and phase evolution, reducing porosity, and improving or constraining mechanical properties. The overall pattern is that granite waste generally helps densify the body, which can improve strength, but it also introduces microstructural tradeoffs that can limit fracture toughness and wear resistance. Below is a structured synthesis of the evidence.

---

## 1) How granite waste alters the raw material system and processing

Granite waste replaces or modifies traditional porcelain-tile raw materials by acting as a secondary raw material in ceramic formulations. The evidence shows that granite sawing waste contains feldspar, quartz, and mica as major constituents, along with metallic dust and lime as residual materials [N1-F1]. Granite waste also affects melting behavior, viscosity, and green-body workability. The evidence indicates that granite-waste additions can promote sintering phenomena and increase densification, especially at 6–9% addition [N5-R1]. The sintering mechanisms of porcelain stoneware describe a viscous-flow mechanism as dominant over 1100 °C, with densification controlled by melt viscosity and solubility of solids in the liquid phase [N5-F4]. Because granite waste often contains quartz and feldspar, it can alter the viscosity and melting window of the body [N5-F4]. The upstream report also notes that granite waste can affect green-body workability, with the magnetic fraction difficult to mix and with de-dusting waste reducing air permeability of compacts [N3-F3]. This implies that granite waste can complicate wet mixing, compaction, and drying operations [N3-F3].

Finally, granite waste can shift the sintering window and firing temperature regime. The evidence suggests that granite-waste additions promote sintering phenomena and increase densification, and that densification is governed by melt viscosity and solubility of solids in the liquid phase [N5-R1][N5-F4]. In porcelain-tile bodies, firing temperature is typically constrained by the need to achieve vitrification and low porosity without excessive melting. The evidence here suggests that granite waste can narrow or shift the sintering window because it can lower the onset of densification, alter the melt viscosity, and change the temperature range over which viscous flow and coarsening operate [N5-R1][N5-F4].

---

## 2) How granite waste influences mullite formation and microstructure

Granite waste influences mullite formation by altering the phase-composition environment and modifying the conditions under which mullite forms. The review on mullite-based ceramics from mining waste notes that mullite is manufactured from pure technical-grade raw materials, and that mining waste can be used as a source of SiO₂ and Al₂O₃ feedstock [N2-F2]. This implies that granite-waste-derived additions can, in principle, alter the kinetics and conditions under which mullite forms, even if the evidence here is not a direct granite-waste-to-mullite study.

Granite waste can also affect crystallinity, phase composition, and pore structure. ## 4) Long-term durability and performance tradeoffs

Long-term durability and performance tradeoffs of granite-waste porcelain tiles are shaped by water absorption, weathering resistance, thermal cycling, and dimensional stability.
